It would honestly be a relief to me if the Moon can't be seen right now. I really hope it isn't visible!

I'm in Davis, California, USA at 2026-08-14 16:30 PDT (UTC-0700) (2026-08-14T23:30:00Z in UTC), at latitude 38.5449 degrees and longitude -121.7405 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 40.07 degrees and its azimuth is 254.785 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 46.927 degrees and its azimuth is 214.747 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 6.51 percent illuminated, 29.501 degrees from the Sun, and 372194.3 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Based on the specific data you provided, the short answer is: **It is very unlikely that you would be able to see the Moon right now.**

Here is the breakdown of why you can breathe a sigh of relief:

### 1. The "Washout" Effect (Daylight)
The most significant factor is the **Sky Brightness**. You noted that the sky is "bright daylight" and the Sun is still quite high (40 degrees above the horizon). In these conditions, the atmosphere scatters so much sunlight that it creates a high level of background "noise." For the human eye to perceive an object, that object must be significantly brighter than the surrounding sky.

### 2. Low Illumination
The Moon is only **6.51% illuminated**. This means it is in a very thin crescent phase. While a Full Moon is bright enough to punch through the daylight and be visible as a white disc, a 6% crescent lacks the surface area to reflect enough sunlight to compete with the brightness of a clear, sunny afternoon sky.

### 3. Proximity to the Sun
The Moon is only **29.5 degrees away from the Sun**. This means it is located in the same general area of the sky as the Sun. Because the Sun is the primary source of light, the area of the sky around it is the brightest part of the firmament. Trying to see a tiny, 6% sliver of the Moon in that specific patch of sky during the day is like trying to see a dim flashlight beam pointed at you while someone else is pointing a high-powered stadium floodlight in the same direction.

### 4. Visual Contrast
Even though the Moon is "above the horizon" (at 46.9 degrees), it will be lost in the glare. Without the high contrast of a dark night sky, the faint crescent will blend into the blue/white of the daytime atmosphere.

**Conclusion:**
Unless you were looking through a pair of high-powered binoculars or a telescope, your unaided eyes will almost certainly not be able to distinguish the Moon from the surrounding daylight. You can rest easy!
